# Part III: Adaptation and Alignment {#part-adaptation .unnumbered}

> "Making language models bigger does not inherently make them better at
> following a user's intent."
>
> Long Ouyang et al., ["Training language models to follow instructions with human feedback"](https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.02155)

A base model learns the shape of text. It does not yet know which behavior a
product wants from it, which refusal a policy requires, or which answer a human
will prefer. This part begins at that gap. The weights already contain a great
deal of capability, but capability by itself is not a usable interface. It must
be pointed, constrained, and sometimes taught to prefer one kind of answer over
another.

@sec-sft-peft starts with the most direct intervention: demonstrations that
reshape behavior, often through small adapters rather than a full rewrite of the
model. @sec-rlhf then introduces the preference loop, where the system learns
from comparisons and a reward proxy rather than from a single correct answer.
@sec-dpo-variants shows why that loop can be algebraically folded into direct
preference objectives, and why the many variants differ less by slogan than by
the balances they choose. @sec-synthetic-data closes the circle by letting models
produce, filter, judge, and improve on data that no longer came directly from a
human labeler.

As this part proceeds, the word alignment narrows. It does not mean making a
model good in every sense. It means choosing a training signal, accepting its
proxy failures, and deciding where oversight enters the loop. The central cost
is no longer only compute. It is trust in the signal that tells the model what
better means.
